howSecured: 1. Online Assessment [ 240 students appeared, 27 selected ] This was an online round, conducted offline at the college, with a duration of 1.5 hours. It consisted of 14 questions: 1 medium-level DSA coding question, 1 easy-level SQL query, and 12 MCQs. The MCQs focused on fundamental concepts of Java, OOPS, and DBMS. Make sure to review the core concepts of OOPS, DBMS, and basic SQL queries. For the coding question, submit your code even ifitonly passes partial testcases. 2. Technical Interview [ 27 students appeared, 15 were selected ] In this round, the interviewer focused mainly on my resume, and the interview lasted about 20 minutes. He began by asking me to share something about myself that wasn't included in my resume. He then asked me to explain each project listed on my resume and the motivation behind them. I explained why I chose each project. I gave an overview of the features, frameworks/languages used, and the event flow for each project. He also asked in-depth questions about the keywords in my project section, like APIs and machine learning models. He asked, "What are APIs?", "What are API response codes?", "What is an API token and why is it important?", and "Have you built an API?" For the college recommendation app I worked on, I explained the ML model, even though it was handled by another team member, emphasizing the need to fully understand all aspects of a project. The interviewer pointed out flaws in my projects, and I explained my approach to fix them and why the issues occurred. For example, in a 24-hour hackathon, time constraints prevented full implementation. He also asked how Iwould implement security layers in each project. We discussed the Flutter framework and Firebase. He asked if I had experience with NoSQL databases, to which I responded that Firebase Realtime Database is a NoSQL database. When asked about AWS and Kafka, I admitted I had read about them but didn't have in-depth knowledge. Lastly, he presented a scenario: if a transaction occurred in Mumbai at 11:20, followed by another in Pune 20 minutes later, how would I detect fraud? I acknowledged that Iwasn't sure of the exact technology to use, but my approach would involve calculating the time difference and distance between the two locations to determine ifthe transaction was possible. For this round, it'simportant to answer honestly. You're not expected to know everything, but relate what you do know to the topic. 3. HR Interview Round [15 students appeared, 13 were selected ] This round was mainly HR-focused, but the interviewer also asked some basic technical questions. Itlasted about 20-25 minutes. He began by asking which programming languages I've worked with. I mentioned that my primary language is C++, but I also have knowledge of Java, Python, and Dart. Then he asked me to explain Object-Oriented Programming, what polymorphism is,where I've implemented it, and the difference between the two types of polymorphism. After that, the HR questions started. He asked what challenges Ifaced during my internship. I explained that I encountered issues deploying the app on the Play Store due to Google policy conflicts, and Idescribed how I resolved those issues. Next, he asked why I chose Barclays and followed up with a few more questions based on my response. He then presented a hypothetical situation: What would I do if a superior said something rude to me in a meeting? He also asked how I would handle itif a junior told me I had spoken rudely to them, and how I would manage two team members arguing during a meeting if I were the team leader. For these questions, ensure your answers align with the company's values. He also asked me to describe a situation where I experienced conflict with teammates and to share an experience where I led a team. I described my experience as the Mudra domain head here. For HR questions, it'simportant to understand the company's values and tailor your answers accordingly. 13 students were offered the Summer Internship.

howSecured: 1. Pre - Placement Talk: 24th June 2. Resume Screening: 27th June 3. Online Aptitude Test: 28th June Further rounds took place offline on 2nd July 4. Group Discussion 5. Interview Round 1 6. Interview Round 2 7. HR Round Resume Screening Your resume is as very crucial a part of the entire selection process as any other. Building your resume is a time consuming process, so allot enough time for it. Try to tailor your resume to the role you are applying for. All resumes are screened by an ATS (Applicant Tracking System), so you can check your score on websites like "ResumeWorded". My resume had a score of 72. Key points regarding resumes - They should be 1 page resumes as that's what is expected from freshers. Make single column resumes in Latex format. Try to include all relevant coursework / competition / projects / internships in your resume. Having 1-2 good finance projects on your resume helps. Participate in case study competitions. Do some finance certifications and add them onto your resume. You can make minor changes to your resume that you are taking for your interviews. Results were announced 1 day prior OA Test around 9. Online Assesment (67 Students were shortlisted) The online test was conducted on campus. With a total of 45 marks, it consisted of 4 sections - Finance & Accounting (10): This section contains mostly accounting and corporate finance questions. I think it had 1 question about puttable bonds. Market Awareness (10): This section contained quite a few economy questions and market sentiment questions, I had something related to " what is the exemption on taxes for investing in government pension schemes", so focus on market situations and terms, be aware of current affairs just to be safe Quantitative Aptitude (15): This section focused on permutations, probability, and algebra questions. So this one is out and out mathematics. Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (10): This is an English section, pretty simple if you try to stick with the basics. The time given was 45 mins, so there is a time crunch as the quant section is tough, the VARC section is easy but time consuming. So try to segregate the sections into time slots so you can attempt as much as possible. The results for this round were announced a day before the final day i.e. 1st July. So don't lose heart in the process and be prepared. Group Discussion (37 students were shortlisted) Group discussion Topic - "Central Banks' Diverging Paths Amid Geopolitical Stress - The Bank of England maintains rates at 4.25% due to global uncertainty, while Norway and Switzerland have opted for rate cuts. Explore how central banks should balance inflation control with growth risks, particularly in the context of conflicts or trade wars." The moderators also introduced subtopics during the discussion. As far as I remember, these included "Views on Forex reserves", "What are the impacts of having different views and policy of central banks" Ensure you contribute at least 3-4 meaningful qualitative points. Try to work as a team, acknowledge others points and add on to it. Make sure you speak for 45 sec - 60 sec per point so the moderator takes note of you. The discussion time was 20 mins and last 10 min were for summary We had 3 panels for GD Interview Round 1 (22 students were shortlisted) The round consisted of accounting questions, Corporate Finance, puzzles, mental maths, market awareness. The following are the questions that were asked to me. The change in depreciation and taxes and what are its effect on the financial statements. Latest IPO and M&A What is capital restructuring and why is it done. I had made a DCF valuation project, so I was asked questions about it. I was asked to calculate 57 × 63. Be sure to explain your approach. Other people were also asked the values of roots i.e 2,3,10 etc. I had done the forage investment banking simulation course, so a few questions on them. The round lasted for 30-40 mins. I was last in panel but was called early which took me by shock. If you are not able to answer anything don't panic makes sure you tell the thought process and approach for it. If you make a mistake or there is some misunderstanding in what you were supposed to answer DO NOT PANIC, --your interview isn't over. One or two mistakes are acceptable so keep your head down and focus on answering the rest of the questions properly. Once the GD is done you might receive the order of interview, but always be ready there can be changes in last minute and you can be called anytime Interview Round 2 (12-15 students were shortlisted) This round was taken by the manager for CIB, the duration of this round was only 7-8 minutes. The round consisted of 30-35 rapid fire questions. I was asked to explain the DCF valuation model I had made. I was also asked questions on WACC, Beta, Financial Ratios, Talk about any stock for 30 seconds--its market capitalisation, stock value any and everything you know about it. I was asked if I invested in stock, to which I answered no. I was able to answer all the questions correctly. Make sure you are thorough with all the formulas. My round 2 was scheduled a minute after my round 1 so be ready. Everything happens simultaneously and can be chaotic, so be relaxed, focused and calm. HR Interview (10 students were shortlisted) This round was informal and relaxed, lasted for 10-15 mins. I was asked to briefly talk about my resume and explain one of my leadership roles. I was asked about my family background. I was asked did I know what exactly my job role is and how my past work and leadership experience can help me to better in the internship. 10 students were selected for CIB banking role Important Tips 1. The core essence of the process is not about how much you know but whatever you do, how well-versed you are in it. So focus on learning things deeply rather than trying to do a lot of things. 2. Resources CFI courses - Accounting Fundamentals, Corporate Finance, Reading Financial Statements Udemy - The complete investment banking 2025 Forage - Jp Morgan Investment banking job simulation YouTube - DCF valuation, How are 3 financial statements linked, 2008 financial crisis, SVB bank collapse, what is SENSEX AND NIFTY, how is GDP calculated, Adani-Hindenburg saga, Puzzles - GFG 100 puzzles Quants- IndiaBix.com 3. During interviews, always maintain proper posture, have a smile on your face, do not panic even if you are unable to answer and at least let the interviewer know what approach you're thinking about. 4. The entire placement cycle is very hectic and stressful but it is important to stay in the present and study without worrying about external factors like market situation, recession, etc. Believe me, it never goes to waste. If you have prepared honestly, you will get opportunities. 5. If you have any questions,, I'll be more than happy to help. You can reach out to me directly on WhatsApp or Linkedin. 1. Aptitude 2. HR round 3. Technical round (CTO + DVP) 4. HR round (again) 1. Aptitude [total 4 people] The aptitude round was one hour long and was divided into four sections - Reasoning, Aptitude, Verbal, and Emotional Intelligence - with 15 questions in each section. Topics covered included compound interest, speed and distance, ratios, and seating arrangements. Time was a constraint, but the questions themselves were manageable and solvable with good preparation. I was able to attempt approximately 10 questions per section. Preparation Tips: Practicing from IndiaBix is more than sufficient for this round. Focus on time management and attempt easier questions first. Regular practice on compound interest, ratios, and seating arrangements is recommended. Important Points to Remember: Do not spend too much time on any single question. Since each section has 15 questions and time is tight, move on quickly if you are stuck and come back if time permits. There was no negative marking. All 4 candidates were shortlisted for the next round. 2. HR round [total 4 people] This was a standard HR round that felt more like a casual conversation than a formal interview. It began with "Tell me about yourself." Other questions asked included how I feel about the work environment at Edelweiss, what I do apart from coding and what my hobbies are, explaining my projects and what problem they solve, and questions about my family background and what my family members do. There was also a discussion about how Edelweiss handles sensitive client data and why they cannot feed such data into LLMs. The HR had also asked me if I've researched about the company and if I have looked up any employees there. One candidate was unfortunately not selected after this round. Preparation Tips: Be confident and conversational. Know your resume thoroughly, especially your projects - be ready to explain what problem each project solves in simple terms. Research the company beforehand so you can speak about their work culture with some awareness. Resume Pointers: Make sure your projects are clearly described with the problem statement and solution. List hobbies that reflect personality and aren't generic. Keep your personal background section ready in your mind even if it's not on the resume. Important Points to Remember: Treat this round as a conversation, not an interrogation. Be natural, smile, and engage genuinely. Knowing basic facts about Edelweiss. 3. Technical round [total 3 people] This round was conducted by the CTO and DVP. The questions covered OOP pillars with a request to give a real-world example from my own project where I applied them, a deep dive into my project and internship experience and how they work, the difference between NoSQL and SQL and a system design scenario where I was asked to build a PolicyBazaar clone and choose an appropriate tech stack. For the PolicyBazaar clone, I suggested React for the frontend and .NET for the backend, reasoning that the existing team would likely be familiar with it. When asked about handling document uploads such as insurance documents, I proposed using a relational database like PostgreSQL where a documents table would have a foreign key referencing the primary key of the users table, and a column storing an array of URL strings pointing to documents stored in a private S3 bucket. Preparation Tips: Revise OOP concepts (Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism) and have a concrete example from your own project ready for each. Be comfortable explaining your projects and internship work end-to-end. Practice basic system design - especially around databases, storage, and API design - as scenario-based questions are common. Resume Pointers: Only mention projects and internships you can speak about confidently and in depth. Be ready to justify every technology choice mentioned on your resume. Important Points to Remember: If you forget something mid-answer, do not panic or go silent. Just continue speaking and move forward. If you genuinely cannot recall something, say so honestly rather than fumbling. Interviewers appreciate composure and clarity of thought far more than a perfect answer delivered nervously. 4. HR round [total 2 people] This final HR round was primarily informational rather than evaluative. The HR representative explained what Edelweiss does as a company and walked me through the benefits of joining, such as access to experienced mentors and growth opportunities within the firm. It was more of an onboarding conversation than a screening round. Preparation Tips: Listen actively and ask thoughtful questions about the role, team structure, or learning opportunities. This is your chance to show genuine interest in the company. Important Points to Remember: Even though this round feels relaxed, remain professional. Show enthusiasm about the opportunity and the company. Asking one or two genuine questions about the role or the team leaves a positive impression. There were 2 groups each consisting of 4 people each. I was a part of the first group and 2 of us had received the offer letter.

howSecured: Placement Process: 1. Online Assessment (OA) 2. Technical Interview Round 3. HR Interview Round 1. Round 1: Online Assessment [ 197 students ] ( 11/07/2025 ) Eligibility: Minimum CGPA of 7.0+ UBS had come to campus in the month of march for selection of students for campus hackathon. For the hackathon they had conducted an online assessment. The shortlisted candidates for campus hackathon were directly eligible for interviews. I was one of them. The assessment was largely the same for both hackathon and placement selections. It included technical MCQs focused on Computer Science fundamentals such as Data Structures & Algorithms, DBMS, and OOPs. There were also questions on error identification, output prediction, and one coding question based on DSA. The coding problem was of moderate difficulty, and I successfully passed all the test cases. A total of 10 were shortlisted. 2 from Second year and 8 from Third year. The hackathon was a really great opportunity for getting to know the work culture at UBS and also connecting with the mentors. For such rounds I recommend to ● Practice aptitude and DSA problems regularly. ● Be comfortable with Java syntax and core concepts of OOP. ● Brush up on CS fundamentals like DBMS, OS, and basic algorithms. ● Focus on accuracy and efficiency during coding questions. 2. [Technical Interview] [ 16 students ] ( 14-07-2025 ) There were a total of 16 candidates selected for this round. ( 15 through OA and 1 hackathon participant ). We were asked to report to campus at 9 am. The interviews started at around 10 am. There were 6 panels for the candidates, and the interviews for Summer interns and placements were held together. They began with placement candidates. They first asked me to introduce myself and to mention all the core subjects that i had till now. I mentioned the Minor course in Banking technology and they seemed interested in it. And he asked me to explain what the course contained and a discussion for 3-5 minutes. Next they moved on to core subjects, asking some questions on OS and some questions on DSA. Then he asked me about my work in the internships and this conversation lasted for 7 - 10 minutes. He asked what exactly the work was about and he asked some in-depth questions regarding different specific implementations. They asked me about my interest in Computer Engineering and why this specific field. I was asked a question about implementation of a monopoly board game in abstract terms, the classes and data structures used. There were few questions on my implementation, I was able to answer all, except one. I was not sure about the question but I mentioned my answer and said that I would be able to append to my answer if I could actually get into implementing it or drafting it. Tips: ● You should know your resume completely, why and where a particular tool, framework or language was used. What was your role in the projects, What is it about and the concepts used in the project. ● For OOPS : java docs and any book about OOP language that covers from the fundamentals (eg. Java programming from the ground up ) ● For Data Structures : college syllabus is sufficient but Being well versed with implementations may be helpful. ● For Algorithms : The problems are doable. Having some consistency is important. You should atleast go through your implementation or the thinking with them, if a direct complete solution does not come to the mind, sometimes even they nudge you into the right direction. ● For DBMS : The questions aren't difficult and online resources are enough for it. 3. [HR Round] [ 9 students ] ( 14-07-2025) This was not like a formal round but more as a casual conversation. It lasted about 10 minutes. They asked some basic questions about my hobbies, how I would describe myself. And then they asked me about my hackathon experience and to describe the environment over at the campus. Then they asked some questions about my internship experience. And that was basically it. The only thing I could say about the HR round is to be confident and be comfortable. Be calm. Finally 3 students were selected for internships.

howSecured: 1. OA - It consisted of 2 Coding Questions 2. 3 Interview Rounds - 2 Technical + 1 HR 1. [Online Assessment] [35 candidates were shortlisted based on Resume] Platform & Duration: The first round was an online proctored assessment conducted on AssessHub. The test was scheduled at 9:00 PM and conducted from home with a total duration of 1 hour. Note: The platform was very strict regarding malpractice. Even attempting to copy-paste code (Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V) triggered alerts. Hence, all code had to be typed manually. Test Pattern: The assessment consisted of 2 coding questions, both of which were logically easy but required clarity of concepts. 1. Encryption & Decryption Program ● Based on ASCII values and bit manipulation ● Required understanding of character encoding and logical operations. 2. Pattern-Based Question ● Print the mirror image and water image of a given pattern Shortlisting: Around 35 students appeared for this round, 9 students were shortlisted for the interview process. 2. [Technical Interview - 1] [Duration: ~ 40-50 minutes] Interview Experience: The interview was conducted by a Platform Engineer (Team Lead) and focused on core fundamentals, problem-solving approach, and mindset. Topics & Questions Asked: 1. Introduction ○ Asked to briefly introduce myself. 2. Core Java Concepts ○ Difference between JVM, JDK, and JRE ○ Why Java is called "Write Once, Run Everywhere (WORE)" 3. Project Discussion ○ Asked to explain how I develop a project from scratch ○ I explained my major project, covering: ■ Problem statement analysis ■ Researching possible solutions ■ Evaluating solutions based on feasibility, viability, and business impact ■ Selecting the tech stack ■ Task division, development, and unit testing 4. Conceptual Question ○ Explained Machine Learning as if explaining it to a 5-year-old (tested clarity of understanding). 5. Coding & Logical Questions ○ Reverse a string (I clarified whether it should be in-place) ○ Complete a number series ○ Write pseudo-code for a pattern 6. Scenario-Based Question ○ Asked whether I would work on a simple or less popular technology even if it may not be useful in the long term ○ This question tested attitude and professionalism, and required a balanced, diplomatic answer Key Takeaways & Tips: ● Always clarify problem statements and edge cases ● Focus on approach, not just the final answer ● Be honest but diplomatic in scenario-based questions ● Communicate clearly and confidently 3. [Technical Interview - 2] [ Duration: ~ 1 hour 15 minutes] Interview Experience: This round was conducted by a Senior Developer and was deeply technical. The interviewer explicitly mentioned that he would go through each item mentioned in my resume. Topics & Questions Asked: 1. Object-Oriented Design ○ Given an employee scenario, asked to: ■ Design class hierarchy ■ Use appropriate data structures ■ Think from a production-level perspective 2. Logical & Coding Questions ○ Add, fetch, and delete employees based on conditions ○ Example: ■ Find employee with highest salary ■ If salaries are same, return the employee who joined most recently 3. DBMS ○ Designed an ER diagram for the employee system ○ Wrote 4-5 SQL queries ○ Differences between SQL and NoSQL ○ Given scenarios and asked which database to use and why 4. Data Structures ○ Code to find the meeting point of two linked lists 5. Internship Discussion (Kafka) ○ Why Kafka instead of simple APIs ○ How Kafka improved efficiency and scalability ○ Where Kafka was used in the project 6. Project-Based Questions ○ Detailed discussion on projects mentioned in my resume Key Takeaways & Tips: ● Know everything written in your resume in depth ● Practice OOP design questions ● Revise DBMS, SQL queries, and linked list problems ● Be prepared to justify technology choices 4. [HR Interview] [ Duration: ~ 20-25 minutes] Interview Experience: This was a conversational round focused on personality, awareness, and fit. Questions Asked: ● Feedback on my previous two interviews ● Names of interviewers (to check attentiveness) ● Internship experience (internships are always a plus) ● Family background ● Willingness to relocate to Pune Overall Feel: The HR round was friendly and more about understanding me as a person rather than testing technical skills. [ 2 students were offered the job ]
prep: ● Striver's DSA Sheet is honestly one of the best resources to practice DSA. If you're confused about where to start, just follow the sheet consistently. ● Keep your fundamentals very clear. No matter how much you code, interviewers always test your basics. ● Just like many others, I initially thought placement preparation means only focusing on DSA. But that's not true. You should prepare SQL queries with the same seriousness as DSA coding. ● For SQL practice, SQL50 is a great place to strengthen your basics. Additionally, I used ChatGPT to generate scenario-based SQL questions and complex queries, which helped me think from an interview perspective. ● For Aptitude preparation, I found CareerRide to be a really good and reliable resource. ● Make sure you revise DBMS and OS fundamentals, as they are frequently asked in interviews. ● And most importantly, communication skills. Even if you know the answer, you should be able to clearly explain your approach and thought process. Interviewers pay a lot of attention to this.

howSecured: Online Assessment Round: (36 Questions 120 minutes) Technical Interview I Technical Interview II HR round 1) Online Assessment Round: The online test was conducted on the HackerRank platform and consisted of 36 questions, including 2 coding problems, several SQL queries, and questions on Operating Systems and Networking. This test was common for both the App Development and Associate Consultant roles, and candidates were shortlisted for the Associate Consultant interview based on their performance. The coding questions varied for each candidate; for me, one of the problems was the Valid Parentheses question, which can be easily solved using a Stack. 2) Technical Round I : [27 students were selected for the technical interview] The interview started after a PPT presentation from Oracle at around 12:00 PM. It began with the question "Tell me something about yourself apart from your resume." Be prepared for this in advance -- try to include your strengths, hobbies, extracurricular activities, and any committee participation. Everything you mention should highlight how effective and valuable you can be for the company. After introducing myself, the interviewer asked me which programming language I was most proficient in. I said Java, as it's my favorite language and I usually solve coding problems in it. She then asked me a few OOPs questions -- what is Abstraction, Polymorphism, why one should learn Java, and why Java is platform-independent. Since we had prepared well for topics like Collections Framework and Multithreading (as Oracle often asks these), I was confident. Next, she asked why I had chosen MongoDB for my projects. I had mentioned both MongoDB and MySQL in my resume, so I explained my choice based on schema flexibility and scalability, describing how MongoDB scales both horizontally and vertically. I also added that relational databases are equally important because they follow ACID properties, ensuring data integrity and security. She seemed very happy with this answer. She then asked about the machine learning algorithms I had used in my projects. One of the questions was to explain Naïve Bayes, which I had used during the initial phase of my project. I didn't give a detailed example but explained how it works and why it's effective. Tip: If you've implemented any functionality, make sure you understand the high-level flow, how you implemented it, and how it actually works in the backend. Later, she asked a few questions on Authorization and Authentication, including how JWT (JSON Web Token) works. After that, she moved on to two basic DSA questions: Swap two numbers without using a third variable. Reverse a string. For on-campus interviews, string-related questions are very common, so make sure to prepare linear data structures thoroughly. Finally, she asked some basic SQL questions -- definitions and the differences between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP commands. Some questions about View how does data in view table get updated even it does not support DML After that, my interview concluded. 2) Technical Round 2: [ around 20 students appeared for it] Round 2 began with a quick greeting, and the interviewer immediately moved to a DSA question, asking for the solution in Java. The problem was: given an array of strings, convert all elements into camel case and then sort them based on the first character of each element. I wrote the complete solution, explained my approach, and he seemed satisfied with my explanation. After that, he asked two simple SQL questions -- one on LEFT JOIN and another on a basic aggregate function. I solved both queries and also mentioned that if a similar question appeared, I could handle it using the GROUP BY clause. Afterward, he reviewed my resume and asked me to elaborate on any one of my projects that I could explain well. I confidently replied that I could explain any of the three projects mentioned in my resume, so he asked me to choose one. I described the project in detail, and he didn't interrupt or cross-question, indicating that my explanation was clear. He then asked a few personal questions -- where I was from and about my role as the Point of Contact for the Alumni and Mentorship Program at SPIT. My advice is to answer such non-technical questions smartly. You can add a touch of personality or humor to make the conversation more engaging and reduce nervousness. Interviewers usually appreciate candidates who are not only technically strong but also have good communication and interpersonal skills. For me, this approach worked really well -- the interviewer became more comfortable, and our interaction felt natural. We both enjoyed the conversation, and overall, the second round went very smoothly for me. Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it] The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities. After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. howSecured: 1. Pre-placement Talk If you're seriously interested in a company, it's really important to attend the PPT and moreover, really pay attention to what exactly they are looking for, information about the role (location, CTC, I+P or not, etc.), company values and what they do. In this case, the role is that of Corporate Trainee and it has further categories like Developer and Data Scientist that they would decide based on our profiles. - You can take note of things you find important and want to remember for interview rounds. - In case of virtual PPTs, keep screenshots of slides with company values, their achievements, skills required etc. 2. Resume Shortlisting This is a very crucial step and many deserving people sometimes fail to get their resume shortlisted (happened with me in certain initial companies) due to ignoring these basic points:- ● CGPA! Even though it cannot compensate for your lack of skills, maintaining a decent CGPA can definitely save you from being eliminated if the company has internal criteria for filtering out candidates. As far as I have seen, having a CGPA of >7.5 is good enough and will make you eligible for all companies. However if you want to guarantee that they don't eliminate you from their side, stay above 8 just in case. (Mine bordered around 7 which was a mistake on my part but I kinda made up for it through my resume and other areas, so luck is a big factor and if you don't have a good CGPA don't get demotivated because many companies look at your overall profile as well). ● ATS! Since it is unclear what the resume shortlisting criteria is for each company, do not think ATS score does not play a role. There may be times when HRs do not want to look through the resumes of 200-300 candidates so they simply filter on the basis of ATS score. So focus on increasing your resume's ATS score as much as you can (>80 on Resume Worded is great), and there are many techniques to do that by including stats, action words, at least 1 work experience and 2-3 good projects that actually add value, leadership roles, etc.) ● JD! Tailoring your resume according to the role and company you are applying for is really important, so please have a good look at the JD provided (things like skills required, role of intern, what the company does) and strategically include things that will give you an advantage when you talk about them during your interview. In my case, the role wasn't very specific like an SDE or DA or a non-tech role so what worked for me was showing versatility through projects and courses/certifications by adding 2 ML/Data Science related projects and 1 deployed fullstack project. Also, I researched a bit about what the company's main business is and accordingly included an AI-based loan underwriting agent project for brownie points. You can get a better idea through my resume that I used for Mahindra Finance: Akshata_Mahindra_Resume.pdf 3. Aptitude Test [~150 candidates got resume shortlisted and attempted this round] This round was conducted on the YUGMA platform and consisted of 100 questions (covering quants, aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal aptitude and behavioral/situation based questions) to be solved in 1 hour. The challenge here was not in the difficulty of the questions but rather effective time management, and also the fact that each question had negative marking as well. I started from the beginning and had solved about 15-20 questions when I realised that there were so many questions to be done in a limited time. I then started solving the behavioral and verbal questions first as they were pretty easy and obvious to answer so they would secure marks, and after covering all those I moved on to the remaining quant questions which revolved around topics like speed distance and time, percentage, profit loss, discounts, etc. which were very doable. Practicing from IndiaBix is more than enough to prepare for aptitude based questions and I also think quick strategising and presence of mind really played a role here. Keeping in mind the negative marking, I left out 10 questions which I was very unsure of. They had purposely included some very indecipherable questions where it wasn't clear what exactly needed to be done. All I can say is just trust your gut and if you really don't know what to do in a question, simply leave it (ofc only in OAs with negative marking). I think ppl who got >70 questions correct were selected after this round. 4. Coding Test [70 candidates shortlisted from previous round] This was conducted on Assesshub and had 2 sections :- - The first section had around 20 MCQs on basic python input/output questions which are very doable if you know Python basics like loops, variables, conditional operators, etc. - The second section had 3 DSA questions (Leetcode easy level) to be solved in Python only. I was able to do these quickly, having been coding in Python since 1st year, but if you are a beginner you can practice with Blind 75 sheet on Neetcode as they have really good solution tutorials in Python. It was a relatively easy coding round as compared to other OAs I had given before, but attention to detail was really important here since for output questions some options were very similar to each other so we needed to read the code and each option properly. Also, the IDE for DSA questions was quite different to usual ones so we had to adapt our code according to the given main function. I was able to solve all 3 DSA questions and almost all MCQs correctly, and I submitted way before the test ended so maybe both speed and accuracy could have been a factor behind shortlisting for next round. 5. Group Discussion (GD) [29 candidates shortlisted from previous round] We were divided into panels of 6 and I was in the first one. Before starting the GD, we were briefed about general rules to be followed and time guidelines (9 mins for discussion + 1 min for concluding). The topic given to us was "Technology : Boon or Bane" and we were strictly told to be either for or against but not both. After getting the topic, we had a minute to gather and jot down our thoughts. Here, I prepared my points according to technology being a great boon since that is what I believe. However once the GD started, I was the 3rd person to speak up and everyone before me had spoken for the motion so I spontaneously decided to speak about technology being a bane and wrote down 2-3 points that came to my mind while others were speaking. While this could have been a mistake, I thought in the moment that if everyone speaks for the motion then it would be a very dull discussion with all of just saying "I agree with you…" , and I trusted in myself to speak on the spot without a lot of preparation so my communication skills helped me here. I presented a different viewpoint and was the only one who spoke against the motion (that possibly caught the interviewers' attention). 6. Personal Interview (PI) [11 candidates shortlisted from previous round] After getting shortlisted from GD, all of us had 2 interviews : technical and HR, neither being eliminatory. They said they would take into account all our scores (aptitude, coding, GD, PI) and accordingly come up with a result in the end. Both the interviews were in no particular order and I had my HR round first: a) HR : This was a 45-minute long, rigorous HR interview where the Head of HR basically wanted to assess our inner personalities and culture fit rather than technical prowess. She started with my family background, upbringing, what all places I have been to, etc. and also asked about which project taught me the most valuable life lessons and which one made me encounter the most challenges and self-doubts, with simultaneous follow-up questions for each. One important thing here was that I remembered their DE&I (Diversity, Equity & Inclusion) framework from the PPT and subtly included these values in my answers. She asked me a lot of questions about my life experiences and lessons I had learnt along the way to know what kind of a person I am. Towards the end I was also asked if I had come across any unethical practices around me and how I had reacted to them. As far as I could make out from her response to my answers, they look for people who know how and when to speak against something so it's always good to have some answer for these questions. Even if you haven't experienced something, have a presence of mind and think of the most suitable response rather than just saying "No" or "I don't know". Towards the end, she asked me if I had anything to ask her and since I had not really prepared for an HR-specific question I just asked "What are the company's expectations from me in terms of beliefs and values if I get selected?" Again I reiterate, it is always better to have some decent response rather than saying "Nothing". b) Technical : This interview also lasted around 40 minutes and revolved around technical and resume based questions in depth. The interviewer was friendly and polite, starting with asking me for a brief introduction and then moving on to my projects and work experience. He focused more on my 'Smart Returns' project and wanted to know how we decided on the problem statement and how exactly we were solving the problem at hand, what the end results are, detailed explanation of the project workflow and how different technologies are integrated together. He then went on to ask me about a case study along similar lines, it was regarding a demand-based shipping feature for orders on Amazon. I explained about a solution through data driven demand forecasting models to predict order volumes for a particular location depending on various factors like age group, economic capacity, geography, etc. He seemed satisfied with my response and asked me how accurate an ML model would be in such a case. I estimated a >80% accuracy since Amazon is a big company operating since long ago so they would have a large customer database hence we would get good accuracy through data analytics. He then asked me how we would handle the 20% inaccurate demand forecasting done by the ML model, and for this I suggested another feature so that the company's customer satisfaction rating and profitability do not get largely affected. He constantly tried to check if I was confident in my responses and finally seemed satisfied with my answer. 5 students got the final offer, and I was extremely grateful to be one of them.

howSecured: 1. Online Assessment [ Students with >=7 CGPA ] The first stage was an online assessment consisting of a single DSA question + 4 logic/Aptitude questions. Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [ 13 students ] The first technical round was conducted online on a coding platform called Meetl. The interview focused on: • Core Java fundamentals • Java Collections Framework • Object-Oriented Programming concepts • DBMS basics • Data Structures and Algorithms I was given two DSA problems: • One was Leetcode easy level. • The second problem was of medium difficulty (roughly LeetCode medium level) . I had to write the code for both problems and explain the logic clearly . After this round, 3 out of the 13 candidates were shortlisted for the next round. 4. Technical Interview Round 2 (Onsite) [3 students] This round was conducted onsite at the company office and was a pen-and-paper coding round. This interview again focused heavily on OOP concepts and Java fundamentals. Some of the questions included: • Explanation of Parent p = new Child() and Child c = new Parent() along with reasoning. • Typecasting in objects. • Lambda functions in Java. • Streams in Java. • Serializable interface. • Questions about my hackathon experiences and projects. After this , the interviewer asked 4 DSA questions 1. Linked List Delete a node in a singly linked list in constant time. 2. Array Problem Find the second maximum element in an array using one pass and constant space. 3. Integer Stream Problem The interviewer described a scenario where a large stream of integers flows into a queue throughout the day, with the constraint that the difference between consecutive numbers is always 1. At the end of the day, we need to answer q queries asking whether a specific number x appeared in the stream, and the requirement was to answer queries in constant time and constant space. 4. Array Partition Given an array, divide the elements into two arrays such that the difference between their sums is minimum . ( time complexity of order 1 ) The problems themselves were not difficult but were slightly tricky and required reasoning/proof . I wrote code for all four problems and explained the logic clearly. The interviewer seemed satisfied with both my OOP explanations and DSA solutions. The next day I received a call from HR saying that the feedback was positive, and I was invited for the next round. 5. Technical Interview Round 3 (Senior Engineering Manager) [ 2 students ] This round was again conducted onsite and a pen-and-paper round . The interviewer was an Engineering Manager who had been with the company for around 11 years. The round began with questions on the Java Collections Framework, after which the discussion went deep into HashMap internals. I had to explain: • How key-value pairs are stored • Load factor • Rehashing • Collision handling • How collision handling worked before Java 8 and after Java 8 After this discussion, I was asked to write a Student class with attributes: • name • id • marks I wrote the class and implemented the constructor. Then the interviewer asked whether we could directly use this class as a key in a HashMap. This question was meant to check my understanding of equals() and hashCode(). I explained: • The default implementations provided by the Object class • How they compare memory references • Why overriding them is necessary for logical equality I then implemented: • equals() using student id • hashCode() accordingly I also explained what would happen if we did not override these methods. Next we discussed: • Comparable vs Comparator • Writing a Comparable implementation • Writing a Comparator for a different custom sorting strategy • What the return values -1, 0, and 1 represent The interviewer then moved to JDBC, which I had not worked with before, so I honestly mentioned that I had not used JDBC. We then discussed SQL concepts, including: • Different types of joins • Database indexing • Data structures used in indexing (B-Trees) Finally, the interviewer asked two logical puzzles: Puzzle 1: 25 Horses and 5 Tracks Find the top three fastest horses. Puzzle 2: 2 Eggs and 100 Floors Determine the highest floor from which an egg can be dropped without breaking. The interviewer was mainly evaluating how I approached the problems and broke them down logically, rather than expecting an immediate answer. I struggled a bit with the horses puzzle, but with some hints I eventually arrived at the solution. I had mixed feelings after this round because the puzzle part did not go perfectly. 6. Technical Interview Round 4 ( Online ) [ 2 students ] After about a week, HR informed us that there would be one final technical round. This round was conducted virtually and had two interviewers: • One senior engineering leader from the US • One engineer from the Mumbai office ( if selected , he/she will be your manager ) This round was more conversational compared to previous rounds. We started with a discussion about my projects and hackathon experiences. I was asked about the most challenging aspects of my projects and how I approached solving them. One interesting question was about a product in the market that I admire or would like to work on , and I spoke about a technology product I had seen on Shark Tank India. The discussion then moved into database concepts, including: • Relational vs Non-relational databases • MongoDB • Redis ( Since I had used in my project ) • Why Redis, despite being very fast, is usually not used as a primary database for large systems I was also given a probability puzzle involving 50 black balls and 50 white balls distributed across two bags , where the goal was to maximize the probability of drawing a black ball. I initially took some time to reason about the problem, and with a hint from the interviewer I arrived at the correct solution. Towards the end of the interview, the discussion became more open -ended. I asked about a concept the interviewer mentioned called the S2 geometry data structure , which is used for geospatial indexing in systems like Google Maps. I also asked what areas a new engineer should focus on during the first few months after joining . Overall I was able to answer all questions in this round , but again felt dumb because I took a lot more time than required on that simple probability puzzle , brain felt saturated at that moment and stopped thinking, but with one hint from interviewer , arrived at the ans . After this round, there was a long silence from the company for around 14-17 days. During this time, another candidate who was interviewing along with me received a call from HR for the HR discussion round, while I did not receive any update. Naturally, I felt that my process might have ended there. However, after around two weeks, I unexpectedly received a call from HR informing me that my profile had been moved to a different team internally, and because of that, I would have to go through two additional technical &/ team rounds which were scheduled immediately on the next day . 7. Technical Interview Round 5 ( Online ) The fifth round was conducted by a manager from the Mumbai office with around 7 years of experience. The interview was relatively short and focused mainly on Java fundamentals and problem solving. He first asked me about the internal working of HashMap, where I explained buckets, key-value storage, hashCode(), equals() , collisions, collision handling, etc. Then he moved to a DSA problem similar to the "Search Suggestions System" problem on LeetCode. Similar to : Leetcode Search Suggestions I came up with a sorting + string prefix matching based solution. O(n^2) and coded the approach and output was correct. Although the problem had a more optimized binary search based approach possible, he did not ask me to optimize further once the logic and output were correct . The round ended after he asked whether I had any questions for him. 8. Technical Interview Round 6 ( Online ) The sixth and final technical round was with a senior engineer from the US team who had around 15 years of experience. This round was very different from the previous ones. It was not focused on coding or rapid-fire technical questions. Instead, it was more of a deep two-way discussion about the team, their domains, systems, and the type of work they do. He spent a significant amount of time explaining the team structure and the backend systems they work on. I asked a few thoughtful questions regarding the domain and one specific question that he appreciated a lot during the discussion. I also asked him what I should focus on learning before joining so that I could reduce the amount of training effort required from the team side once I joined. He seemed to like that question as well, and the overall interaction was very positive and engaging. The conversation lasted for around one hour. After these rounds, I received a call from HR stating that all interviewer feedback was positive and that the final HR discussion round was scheduled. The HR round mainly covered resume overview, family background, relocation, future plans, joining timeline, and compensation discussion. Toward the end of the HR round, I was also introduced to the manager(same person who took my second last interview) of the team I would potentially join, and we discussed the team goals and what I should focus on before joining. After the HR round, there was another waiting period because the profile had to go through final approval from the US side. howSecured: Process Date: 11th Sept 2025 (OA), 12th Sept 2025 (Interviews) 1. Resume Shortlisting (~100 students appeared) So the process started with resume shortlisting. Rotate array by 2, then you get a string, and if you find any element from that string in your array, replace it with the given element. Technical Interview Round 1 (10 students appeared) I started by introducing myself. They immediately dived deep into my projects, which I had prepared for. Then they gave me the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II problem. I already knew it from Striver's DP sheet, so I explained the DP approach confidently. They then asked for the O(n) linear approach -- I explained but made a small mistake. They kindly corrected me and said, "You're on the right track." That encouragement boosted my confidence mid-interview. They also asked me about the difference between React and normal HTML/CSS and some questions related to my resume . Then came a rapid-fire round: factorial (loop & recursion), recursion issues (I said TLE), which DS recursion uses (Stack), why use DP, assigning priority to objects (I said priority queue). I liked this part because it felt like a fun quiz rather than grilling. Some other candidates were asked to open Google Colab do some visualizations/operations on dataset; I wasn't asked that. Overall, my interview went well. Shortlist: 5 students. 4. Technical Interview Round 2 (5 students appeared) We started again with a quick intro and discussion of one of my hackathon projects. Then they gave me a case study: "You're a Senior Data Analyst at AuxoAI. Microsoft needs 1000 applicants for a job. You have job seeker data from your client. How would you select 1000 candidates for that job role?" I gave some thought then I said I'd parse resumes using pyresparser and extract features like skills, education, location, and experience, and a few more features that I don't clearly remember now.. My output would be "Eligible/Not Eligible." I initially said Naive Bayes for the model. Then they asked how I'd handle candidates backing out at the last moment. At first, I overcomplicated it -- I said I would check factors like college tier (if someone is from a top college, they might get better offers), location preferences, salary expectations, and experience level. I thought of approaching it with regression, reasoning that more experienced candidates usually want better opportunities. But they immediately pointed out that this is actually a classification problem. You can use tools like ResumeWorded to assess your resume and identify areas for improvement. Mind it that this is for cross-checking your resume, don't waste time tailoring it to perfection. Academic performance, including 12th-grade marks and CGPA, can also influence shortlisting, depending on the company's eligibility criteria. Meeting the required cutoffs can be an advantage, but selection also depends on your projects, technical skills, resume relevance, and the overall applicant pool. Online Assessment [ 30 students ] The OA was from home at 4-5 pm, MCQ format and of 30 questions. The OA covered DSA (binary trees, sorting algorithms, and Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's algorithm), Operating Systems (disk scheduling, CPU scheduling using SJF, and inode structures), and DBMS (functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, and normalization forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF). It also included Computer Networks, focusing on the OSI model and the Presentation Layer, along with C++ programming concepts such as destructors, global and local variables, object creation, and output tracing. 3. Group Discussion [ 30 students ] 3 groups of 10 people My topic was 'Are exams right way to assess someone's intelligence' The discussion lasted about 20 min where last 3 min where given to conclude your points Always try to initiate the discussion or be in the first 3 people to start the discussion to catch the panelists attention. 2 mins time is given beforehand to jot down the points before the discussion. Write brief bullet points and pros and cons and do not pick a side as it is a discussion and not a debate. 4. Technical + Hr Interview [15 students ] I was the first one to give the interview so I had no idea what type of questions were asked by the panelists. There were two panelists The interview started with a brief introduction and a walkthrough of my resume. Towards the end of my introduction i stated that would you like me to elaborate on one of my projects technicalities, setting the tone of the interview in my favour. They asked surface level questions on each of my projects and then deep-dived into one of my projects. I was asked if the database was static or dynamic if static what changes would you make, if i want to migrate the data, how would I do it safely without causing a downtime issue. I was asked how would you design a website where many students are filling a form and high traffic shouldn't affect the web app. Then i was asked if i click on a login button what happens in the backend behind the scenes in depth. After a while I was comfortable with the panelists and was confident with my answers. Then they asked behavioral questions like if a team mate is calling sick with a deadline for your project how would you handle the situation. And if a project cannot be completed before the deadline what measures would you take. They also asked me about why you chose this branch and why not CSE/CE. --- PAGE 3 --- The key to a good interview is to remain composed before you answer. I know it's better said than done, but as I had given 2 interviews and a group discussion before this company I was aware of the body language, tone and familiarity with the interview room. Never use negative words like not, no, I am not aware etc. Always use positive alternatives like I am yet to explore this area, I am yet to have hands-on experience in this technicality etc. Do not get excited if you know the answer to a question, take a pause, assess your thoughts and start from the basics and stretch it with all the technicalities you are aware of and relate it with your resume. Rapid Fire Round [ 72 candidates appeared for this round ] This was the first round, and we were all asked to arrive by 8:25 am, and were asked to assemble in 103 by 8:50 am. We thought that we would first receive instructions on how the rapid fire round would be like. But at 9 am sharp, we all receive an email, containing a google form link, and one of the WorkIndia coordinators comes into the room, and tells us to start the test immediately, and that the form will stop taking submissions after 9:15 am. So make sure you have your wifi and laptop battery charging setup. Luckily I was already connected to the wifi and had my laptop charged, so I was able to start the test immediately. Some questions on basic OS and CCN like deadlocks and DNS, some github commands like listing all branches, stash and pop. Some questions on prefix and postfix increment operators, and some basic data structure questions like which data structure is LIFO, FIFO. The objective is to answer as many questions as you can within 15 min. It contained around 40 to 50 questions. I was able to answer all of them, some with a little uncertainty, and submit. 2. Debugging Round [ 46 candidates appeared for this round ] For this round, we had to join the meet link on our laptop. The interviewer then asked whether I prefer Django or NodeJs. I chose Django. Then he sent a link to a small existing django codebase containing an Attendance Tracker project, with a README file containing instructions on what was to be performed. Initially, while starting the server, there were 2 bugs that were required to be fixed. One bug was in the models.py, a syntax error in the choices parameter passed to a models. CharField. Expected syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=[('active', 'Status active'), ('inactive', 'Status inactive')]) Given syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=['active', 'inactive']) The second bug was in the views.py, another syntax error in which the key of a python dictionary was being accessed incorrectly. Expected syntax: [s["name"] for s in students] Given syntax: [s.name for s in students] After fixing the errors, I started the server. The server was running now. After this, I was asked to implement an API endpoint to mark a student's attendance. For this, I was initially adding an attendance field in the existing Student table. But the interviewer asked me for a better way. So I made a separate table, Attendance, which can contain the student_id as foreign key and a date field, to store when the attendance was marked. Then, there was another constraint that a student cannot mark attendance again on the same date. For this, I used the unique_together model option within a Meta class to make the composite field (student_id, date) unique. The interviewer was happy with this. Then I started implementing the API endpoint, and wrote the url and the handler function. But time was running short, so the interviewer just asked to write a comment inside the handler function on how I would implement the endpoint. Throughout the round (around 45 min), I kept telling the interviewer my thoughts and the steps I am taking. Also, googling and using stack overflow was allowed, but no LLMs. The interviewer will judge you based on your knowledge of the programming language, the backend framework, and most importantly your ability to ask the right questions and google them, and find out the answers. I had googled the syntax for using choices parameter, the syntax for implementing the unique together and also the date field. 3. DSA Round [ 15 candidates appeared for this round ] The DSA Round was also conducted in online interview form, and we had to write code on google docs. The questions were of leetcode easy and medium difficulty. The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. Make sure you have a proper introduction ready, which briefly covers your education, your internship experience and high impact projects. Also, create an introduction which aligns with the company's principles. First question: You are given a positive integer N. Find X such that the sum from 1 to X-1 equals the sum from X+1 to N. For this, I first suggested the brute force algorithm of iterating through all elements from 1 to N, then for each element, running 2 for loops to calculate the 1-X-1 and X+1-N sum, giving a O(n^2) TC. I then optimized it by suggesting a prefix sum approach. First, we calc the total sum using the sum of n natural numbers formula, and then iterate from 1 to N, calc prefix sum, and subtract from total sum. So whenever left and right sum become equal, we return that element X. I wrote this code, then the interviewer then told me to optimize it further. So I suggested a binary search approach, and conditions would be if leftSum>rightSum, e=mid-1 and if leftSum<rightSum, s=mid+1, else return mid. Also, I was asked to optimize space complexity as well, so I used the same formula to calculate leftSum (1 to X-1 sum), instead of prefix array. I wrote this code, then the interviewer asked to optimize it even further. I took some time, but thought that if I want to optimize from O(logn), there must be a direct formula. Thats when it clicked me, that I can write an equation, and solve it for X. leftSum = rightSum (x-1)x/2 = totalSum - leftSum - x (x-1)x/2 = n(n+1)/2 - (x-1)x/2 - x (x-1)x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 - x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 = n(n+1)/2 X = sqrt(n(n+1)/2) The interviewer then asked, what does this signify. I said that X will be the sqrt of sum of the n natural numbers. He was happy with this, and explained me that for a solution to exist, the sum of the n natural numbers must be a perfect square. Second Question: https://leetcode.com/problems/majority-element/description/ I first suggested a brute force approach by creating a hashmap (dictionary in python) and storing the frequency of all elements. Then iterating through the hashmap, and returning the element whose frequency is greater than n/2. The optimal approach with constant space complexity is Moore's Voting Algorithm. Majority Element - Leetcode 169 - Python During the DSA round, I was asked why I preferred using Python. I explained that I initially used C++ and had solved around 150 questions on LeetCode in it. But later, I switched to Python because its simpler syntax allowed me to focus more on understanding the logic behind each problem, rather than the boilerplate code. This helped me improve my problem-solving skills more effectively. Tip: If you switch languages for DSA, be clear about your reason, it's not about which language is "better", but what helps you learn and think better. Third Question: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-a-repeating-and-a-missing-number/ For this, I was only able to suggest the approach with the frequency array / hashmap. Then the interviewer gave me a hint that I can modify the array in-place. I started thinking along those lines, maybe swapping the numbers. But time was up, and I wasn't able to optimize it. Schema Design Round [ 7 candidates appeared for this round ] In this round, I was given a problem statement of an Ecommerce Platform on google docs, along with its various requirements. Also, 2 bonus requirements were given of implementing coupons for orders, and a referral system. Initially, I focused on the main requirements, and identified the main entities from them. I wrote down the table names. Then I started building the relations between these tables, with the help of foreign keys, along with the necessary attributes for each of them. While building the schema, I made sure to obey the normal forms like 1NF and mentioned these terms while making the schema. Make sure that you keep properly explaining the interviewer your thought process behind each and every step, and also make sure to ask doubts on things that might not be clear in the problem statement. I had asked some questions, like should I also focus on the merchant's side, or only on the customer's side, and difference between inventory and warehouse, as it was not very clear from the problem statement. Explain the cardinality of each relationship you are creating (one-one, one-many, many-many). After creating a rough schema, the interviewer then identified certain areas that could be improved, normalized further. I listened thoroughly and made these changes, and explained how this approach would be more effective in preventing data redundancy. I was then asked to write 2 SQL queries on the schema I had built. This included finding the delivery times of the recent orders, along with their delivery locations. I used JOIN, ORDER BY, LIMIT, DATEDIFF function for subtracting the placed_at from the delivered_at. Then I was asked to find the average delivery time, for which I used the aggregate function. As I had time remaining, I also went ahead and implemented the bonus requirements. The referral table would be a unary, many-many relationship, and contains referred_by and referred_to (both foreign keys to User table) Finally, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. I asked him what his first six months at WorkIndia were like. He mentioned that he had joined recently, and that while the initial weeks can be hectic, things become smoother as you get familiar with the processes. I shared my own experience from an internship at a startup, where the first couple of weeks were also hectic for me, since I was learning a new tech stack while working on live features. But once I got used to the codebase, I was able to contribute meaningfully and build exciting features. That sense of solving real-world problems was deeply satisfying. The interviewer appreciated this and mentioned that I would be a good fit for a startup like WorkIndia. I would advise learning CTEs while solving SQL 50, because they are a powerful way of dividing your SQL query into manageable and easy-to-understand sequential steps. 5. Culture Round [ 4 candidates appeared for this round ] The culture round felt more like a meaningful conversation than an interview. The interviewer was very friendly, and there's truly no need to be nervous. We spoke about my journey, passions, values, and experiences. It was a heart-to-heart. The questions covered: ● What got you into this field? Why engineering and not any other role? ● Tell me about your journey so far, your internship, and what you learned from your peers. ● Lowest point in your life and academics. ● Your family, your interests, your short- and long-term goals. ● What do you consider as "good work"? I answered honestly, sharing how I got into tech through PC gaming and modding, inspired by my grandfather's tech-savviness. I spoke about learning QBasic in school, then Java, and how my love for coding naturally led me to engineering, where I could solve real-world problems and innovate. I reflected on my regret of not joining any committee in first year, which limited my exposure, but after second year, I made it a point to step out of my comfort zone: applying for internships, connecting with people on LinkedIn, and seeking out opportunities. I also shared my internship experience, the meaningful features I built, and how much I learned from my mentors and colleagues. I opened up about my family's support, and my goal to help them by becoming financially independent and making them proud. When asked about what "good work" means to me, I shared how participating in hackathons changed my perspective. Earlier, good work meant building something cool solo using a new tech. But through hackathons, I realized that true good work is about team collaboration, communication, and building something together that no one could have done alone. It's about leveraging each person's strengths, validating each step as a team, and delivering something meaningful as one unit. Finally, I asked the interviewer: ● How did WorkIndia start, and what impact were you hoping to create? ● How do you deal with scam jobs on the platform? ● From the core values in the WorkIndia PPT, which one do you consider most important? It was a genuine and fulfilling conversation where I could truly be myself. Tip: Don't prepare scripted answers. Reflect on your journey, speak from the heart, and be honest. This round isn't about checking boxes, it's about understanding who you are and what drives you. Also, have a good idea about the companies that you have interned at. The interviewer might ask certain questions like when was the company founded, or how old was your mentor in the company, not to grill you, but to verify authenticity and see how well you know your own experiences. Be honest, and don't try to bluff. It's totally okay to say "I'm not sure" rather than guess. 2 students were offered the role. It was a long day, and the results weren't announced immediately.
